learning_objective: 🎯 Explore how our incredible brain encodes, stores, and retrieves information, and find out the scientific reasons behind why we sometimes forget!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Memory works like a computer in three steps: Encoding (taking in info), Storage (saving it over time), and Retrieval (bringing it back to mind when needed).

Information passes through three stages: Sensory Memory (lasts less than a second), Short-Term Memory (lasts around 30 seconds, limited capacity), and Long-Term Memory (permanent, unlimited capacity).
Divided into Declarative (facts/events) and Non-declarative (skills/habits). Declarative is further split into Episodic (personal life events) and Semantic (general knowledge and facts).
We forget due to Trace Decay (memory fades over time), Interference (new memories block old ones, or vice versa), and Retrieval Failure (the info is there, but we lack the right cues to access it).
Memory is not a video recording. We reconstruct our memories every time we recall them, meaning they can be distorted by schemas, beliefs, and post-event information.

fun_activity.title: 🧩 The Chunking Challenge
fun_activity.instructions: Look at these numbers for 3 seconds: 1-9-4-7-2-0-0-7-2-0-2-3. Turn away and try to write them. Hard? Now group them by years: 1947, 2007, 2023. Try again. Grouping information into 'chunks' magically expands your short-term memory!

exam_tips: 📌 Atkinson and Shiffrin proposed the famous Stage Model of Memory.
📌 Differentiate clearly between Episodic Memory (I remember my 10th birthday) and Semantic Memory (I know the capital of India).
📌 Mention 'Mnemonics' as a strategy to enhance memory (using acronyms, rhymes, or mental imagery).
quick_recap: ⭐ Short-Term Memory can hold roughly 7 (plus or minus 2) items at a time.
⭐ Proactive interference is when old learning disrupts new learning; Retroactive is when new learning disrupts old learning.
⭐ Hermann Ebbinghaus was a pioneer in memory research and created the 'Curve of Forgetting'.
